There are a lot of reasons why the game might be crashing that have nothing to do with Bethesda. It could be their fault, I don't know your situation and you've given no details, but the game runs fine for most people. Given the information it could be anything from your OS security getting in the way, you overmodding or trying to run mods that conflict, you trying to mod beyond your hardware capabilities, not having the hardware to run the game at the settings you're trying to, not sorting your mods properly, or just a corruption of game files that can be caused by any number of things.

I'm not trying to be insulting here, but I can't assume that you know what you're doing or how to troubleshoot a game that doesn't work, especially if you're trying to mod it and don't really know how. Given the limited information you've given so far, that seems the simplest explanation.

If you don't want to deal with the game on PC anymore that's your decision. Bethesda RPGs aren't known to be incredibly stable on any platform, and yes a lot of that is on them and their poor coding. Something that is much easier to fix on PC with unofficial patches and such. Thing is, you do kind of have to learn how to install that stuff and mod the game correctly, and I completely understand not wanting to bother with that. It's not as simple as just slapping it on in many cases, and things like load order and dealing with conflicts are things you have to learn if you really want to get into seriously modding a game.

At any rate, no, console modding is not going to be the same as it is on PC. Console modding is far more limited. You have a limited amount of space to install mods on, and mods that require external files inserted into the game or other programs, such as Script Extender, and large texture replacers are not going to happen. You're not going to be able to slap 4k textures on everything on the consoles or completely overhaul a game. Mostly it'll be things like gameplay tweaks, quest mods, cheats, and item mods.

There are also content restrictions because of Bethesda.net. No nude mods or other sexual content for example. There are other restrictions as well, read the ToS on Bethesda.net to learn more.

It's better than it would be for console gamers, but still not going to be anything near what PC players can do with the games and mods. PC is a lot more open, can use things like Script Extender, SweetFX, and ENB, and doesn't have content restrictions because of a restricted and exclusive outlet. PC modders can choose from a number of sources for their mods, console gamers will only have what's available through Bethesda.net.

If console is your preference that's cool. Mods will exist to extend the game's life and improve the game experience. It's a good thing to have them. However, you should understand that while better than just only having access to the base game as is, it's just not going to match what you can do on a PC when modding these games on any console system, and it's not just a question of system resources. There are other restrictions based on the closed system OS and distribution system for the mods themselves as well.

If you have a console already and enjoy playing there, mods will make things even better. However, if you're really interested in seriously modding games without restriction, then you need to stick with PC. You also need to learn how to do it, Mods are on the whole not 'plug and play' and need to be tweaked and properly installed to work correctly, and many have complicated install instructions. Sometimes conflicts force you to choose between mods because they often don't work together, and sometimes you can use special tools to merge files or adjust the load order to get things how you want. Tools like that are another thing console mods won't be able to take advantage of.

You also need to learn how to troubleshoot the game itself when it breaks, because if you're modding a lot that's going to happen sometimes. Sometimes because of file flubs, sometimes because of unforeseen conflicts, and sometimes even official patches and updates will completely hose a heavily modded game. There are lots of online resources to learn about all that are available.

Modding on PC is a time consuming process that you need to learn how to do properly. If that doesn't interest you or you just don't have the patience to deal with that, a console and the more limited modding provided by it are a good alternative.

If you're seriously interested in really getting into modding a game heavily, Google is your friend and you should spend a lot of time researching how to handle it properly and how to clean up the mess when things go wrong, because eventually they will.
